Lifeline is a territorial strategy game for two players (Black and White) that is played on the cells of an initially empty hexhex board. The recommended board sizes are between 3 and 12 cells per side.

The game was invented by Michael Amundsen and Luis Bolaños Mures. Although inspired by Go, it bears a significant resemblance to Kanare Kato's Meridians.

				
				
					DefinitionsA group is an entire set of connected stones of the same color. A single stone, not connected to others of its color, is also a group.

A group is dead if there is no path of connected empty cells between that group and any other group of its color. The path does not need to be a straight line.

				
				
					PlayBlack plays first, then turns alternate. On your turn, perform the following actions in order:


     Place a stone of your color on an empty cell. If it is your first turn of the game, perform this action twice.
     Remove all dead enemy groups.
     Remove all dead friendly groups.


The board positions at the start and at the end of your turn must be different. In other words, if the only stone you remove is the one you just placed, your placement is illegal.

The last player to make a placement wins. Note that, after your first turn, you will always have a placement available unless you have no groups on the board.

To make the game fair, White will have the option, on their first turn only, to swap sides with Black instead of making a regular move.

—description from the designers

[Rating: 5/10] I know games like this have their fans, but I am not one of them.  It is slow moving.

[Rating: 5/10] An odd one, could go up or down in rating with plays (though might not get them). It's a connection game where Pyrrhic victories are possible (maybe even easy?)  if you use up too much space winning a battle. That brings some interest, some concerns otherwise very unusual for connection games... but also some feelings of futility.

[Rating: 6/10] An interesting game. It has a lot of rules similarity to Meridians. In some ways I like Lifeline more. The game is not decided as easily in the mid-game. In other ways, I find Meridians more interesting in terms of what it has to offer strategically. I would happily play either. They don't feel very similar outside of basic rules. It is much more difficult to capture groups in Lifeline which tends to push into the end game.

[Rating: 6/10] A game similar to Go, but its played a hexagon board and you don't need to tightly surround your opponents pieces. Just cutting off a group from other groups of your opponent is enough to capture and remove them. Nor can new groups be started without being able to find a path to another one of your group. The loser is the first player to run out of valid moves. The games alright. The first couple times I played it, it ended quite suddenly from a dumb mistake. [Rating: 6/10] Not bad. Feels close to Go and Hex, with ideas of Life/Death and Hex-like connection making. I think there's a lot of depth here, but it's not the type of abstract that would hold my attention for very long. It's a bit plodding and tensionless early, and predetermined without many tactics in the endgame.

[Rating: 6/10] Superficially this resembles [thing=333775]Meridians[/thing]—something that is called out in the BGG description for [thing=358196]Lifeline[/thing]. The differences are in what constitutes a dead group ([thing=333775]Meridians[/thing] requires line of sight) and when stones are removed ([thing=333775]Meridians[/thing] removes dead enemy groups at the beginning of your turn).  But I think [thing=333775]Meridians[/thing] and [thing=358196]Lifeline[/thing] play totally differently. That's one of the things I find most interesting about abstracts: a small change in rules can have dramatic effects.

[Rating: 8/10] Simple, quick to play, deep, and engaging. The path rule has more nuance than might first meet the eye.

[Rating: 10/10] A really excellent abstract game. Playing it at different board sizes gives very different experiences. I would start with a 4 or 5 sized board and graduate up to the larger sizes.  To my limited understanding the game is being able to form an eye (while preventing your opponent from doing so, but building the structure joins groups together and in turn can make your position weaker until it is completed.  Very high level play may end up being a degenerative tit for tat, but I've only played it 15 to 20 times, and it's still very interesting to me.
